stem: A team first measures the proportion of employees who retain the preselected pension contribution. It then develops a practical enrollment procedure to help employees choose contributions suited to their goals. Which perspectives correspond to these two tasks?

choices.text: Normative, then prescriptive
choices.rationale: The second classification fits. The first task measures what employees do rather than determining which contribution they ought to choose.

choices.text: Descriptive, then prescriptive
choices.rationale: Measuring actual choices is descriptive; developing practical support for better choices is prescriptive. Descriptive decision research also includes explaining why people choose as they do. Such explanations can inform a prescription without themselves recommending a change.

choices.text: Descriptive, then normative
choices.rationale: The first classification fits. The second task concerns a usable intervention; a normative task would specify the standard by which choices should be judged.

choices.text: Normative, then descriptive
choices.rationale: The first task measures behavior rather than defining a standard, and the second designs practical support rather than describing existing choices.

choices.text: Prescriptive, then normative
choices.rationale: Measuring behavior does not prescribe a change. The second task develops a practical procedure rather than specifying an ideal choice under stated assumptions.

stem: A buyer uses reliable information and her stated priorities to select a supplier. An unforeseeable flood then closes that supplier. What follows about the original decision?

choices.text: The buyer should have given every supplier an equal rating.
choices.rationale: Equal ratings ignore relevant differences.

choices.text: The buyer's priorities must have changed after the purchase.
choices.rationale: The outcome supplies no evidence of a preference change.

choices.text: The flood shows that the buyer assigned incoherent probabilities.
choices.rationale: An unlikely event can occur under coherent beliefs.

choices.text: Its quality depends only on the eventual delivery failure.
choices.rationale: This confuses a bad outcome with a bad process.

choices.text: Its quality depends on the information available when made.
choices.rationale: Evaluate the process using what could reasonably be known then.

stem: A team compares two offices carefully but never considers remote work, although it is feasible. At which stage does the clearest omission occur?

choices.text: Predicting commuting time
choices.rationale: The omission concerns an option, not a forecast about it.

choices.text: Valuing staff satisfaction
choices.rationale: No evidence says satisfaction was misvalued.

choices.text: Implementing the selected lease
choices.rationale: The omission occurred before implementation.

choices.text: Learning from the office move
choices.rationale: Feedback comes after this missed alternative.

choices.text: Constructing the options under consideration
choices.rationale: A feasible alternative never entered the comparison.

stem: Two people can choose either of two jobs. They agree about each job's pay, hours, and risks, but prefer different jobs. Which difference can explain their choices within the rational-choice benchmark?

choices.text: The salary each expects the higher-paying job to provide
choices.rationale: The two people agree about the pay offered.

choices.text: The working hours each predicts for the two jobs
choices.rationale: The two people agree about working hours.

choices.text: The set of jobs each is able to accept
choices.rationale: Both can accept either job.

choices.text: The probability each assigns to the stated employment risks
choices.rationale: Their assessments of the risks are held equal.

choices.text: The importance each assigns to income relative to free time
choices.rationale: Shared forecasts can be evaluated using different priorities.

stem: An annual subscription can be described as “€10 per month, billed annually” or “€120 per year.” Which finding challenges description invariance?

choices.text: Random assignment produces a reliable purchase-rate difference between the two descriptions.
choices.rationale: Equivalent descriptions should produce the same choices under description invariance.

choices.text: Customers purchase more often after the annual fee falls from €120 to €100.
choices.rationale: The price reduction changes the monetary consequence of subscribing.

choices.text: Customers purchase less often after learning that fewer services are included.
choices.rationale: New information about the service can change its valuation.

choices.text: Customers with different usage needs purchase at different rates under one description.
choices.rationale: Different preferences can explain this difference without violating description invariance.

choices.text: Customers purchase at different rates when billing changes from annual to monthly.
choices.rationale: Payment timing changes the consequences, not merely their description.

stem: During a free evening, Amir can accept a paid shift worth €70 to him, attend a concert worth €50 to him, or stay home worth €30 to him. These values already include all costs. What is the opportunity cost of attending the concert?

choices.rationale: This is the value of the chosen activity.
Staying home is not the best alternative.
The paid shift is the best feasible alternative forgone.
Opportunity cost is not the sum of forgone alternatives.
This is the net disadvantage relative to the shift.

stem: A firm paid a nonrefundable €6,000 deposit. Completing the project now costs €2,000 and yields a certain €3,000 benefit; cancellation yields nothing further. Which choice maximizes its remaining net benefit?

choices.text: Cancel; the total historical cost exceeds €3,000.
choices.rationale: The nonrecoverable deposit is not changed by today's choice.

choices.text: Complete; the remaining net benefit is €1,000.
choices.rationale: Compare future benefits and avoidable future costs.

choices.text: Cancel; completion must yield more than €6,000 now.
choices.rationale: That threshold incorrectly counts the sunk deposit again.

choices.text: Complete; recovering the deposit requires finishing.
choices.rationale: The deposit is unrecoverable under either action.

choices.text: Be indifferent; both choices lose the original deposit.
choices.rationale: Their future payoffs differ by €1,000.

stem: A school estimates that smaller classes improve test scores, then debates whether those gains justify losing music lessons. Which distinction best describes these two tasks?

choices.text: Predicting consequences, then evaluating a trade-off
choices.rationale: The first concerns what happens; the second concerns what matters.

choices.text: Constructing alternatives, then measuring sunk costs
choices.rationale: Neither task concerns an unrecoverable past expense.

choices.text: Estimating opportunity costs, then testing class-size effects
choices.rationale: The effect estimate comes first in the stem.

choices.text: Evaluating a trade-off, then predicting consequences
choices.rationale: This reverses the roles of the two tasks.

choices.text: Implementing a choice, then recording its outcome
choices.rationale: No choice has yet been implemented.

stem: A manager treats a supplier's requested delivery date as a fixed constraint. The supplier says a later date is acceptable for a small discount. What should change first in the decision analysis?

choices.text: Treat the requested date as an unrecoverable cost.
choices.rationale: A request is not a sunk expenditure.

choices.text: Choose the smallest discount before valuing timing.
choices.rationale: The package must be evaluated on both dimensions.

choices.text: Keep the date fixed and compare only supplier names.
choices.rationale: That discards a newly feasible trade-off.

choices.text: Add feasible packages combining dates and prices.
choices.rationale: A negotiable term expands the feasible set.

choices.text: Assume every delivery date is now equally acceptable.
choices.rationale: Negotiability does not erase limits or price differences.

stem: A risk-neutral firm chooses A (certain profit €60) or B (€100 in a good market, €0 otherwise). Good and bad markets are equally likely. What is the maximum price of perfect information before choosing?

choices.rationale: This is the total expected profit with information, not its increment.
Without information choose A for €60; with it earn 0.5×100 + 0.5×60 = €80.
This is B's expected profit without information.
This is the difference between A and B's current expected profits.
This is the gain in the good state, before probability weighting.

stem: While searching a display for a particular serial number, an operator fails to notice an unexpected warning symbol that remains visible. Which phenomenon is most directly illustrated?

choices.text: Change blindness
choices.rationale: No before-and-after change is specified.

choices.text: Mere exposure
choices.rationale: Repeated exposure and liking are not the issue.

choices.text: Hindsight bias
choices.rationale: The operator is not reconstructing a past prediction.

choices.text: Anchoring
choices.rationale: No starting numerical estimate is involved.

choices.text: Inattentional blindness
choices.rationale: Attention to one task can exclude an unexpected visible object.

stem: During a brief screen interruption, a chart's legend changes color. A viewer looking at the chart fails to detect the alteration. What is the closest description?

choices.text: Probability neglect
choices.rationale: No probability is being evaluated.

choices.text: Confirmation bias
choices.rationale: The stem specifies no favored belief.

choices.text: Loss aversion
choices.rationale: There is no comparison of losses and gains.

choices.text: Bottom-up capture
choices.rationale: Capture would mean the stimulus attracted attention.

choices.text: Change blindness
choices.rationale: The failure is to notice a change across views.

stem: A commuter deliberately searches for platform numbers, then looks toward a sudden loud crash. Which sequence is illustrated?

choices.text: Two instances of deliberate top-down selection
choices.rationale: The unexpected crash is not the current search goal.

choices.text: Top-down selection followed by bottom-up capture
choices.rationale: A goal guides the first search; an abrupt stimulus drives the second shift.

choices.text: Two instances of post-choice rationalization
choices.rationale: Neither involves explaining a completed choice.

choices.text: Two instances of perceptual change blindness
choices.rationale: Both examples concern directing attention rather than missing changes.

choices.text: Bottom-up capture followed by top-down selection
choices.rationale: This reverses the sources of the shifts.

stem: Reviewers routinely overlook maintenance costs buried in procurement files. Which redesign most directly makes that evidence enter the comparison?

choices.text: Require a maintenance-cost field beside each purchase price.
choices.rationale: The neglected attribute becomes visible at the comparison point.

choices.text: Display the supplier's logo beside the final score.
choices.rationale: The logo is unrelated to the neglected cost.

choices.text: Move the purchase price into a larger typeface.
choices.rationale: This further privileges the already salient attribute.

choices.text: Ask reviewers to remember all previous procurements.
choices.rationale: An unspecific memory demand does not expose the missing evidence.

choices.text: Add a longer general introduction to each file.
choices.rationale: More text need not direct attention to maintenance.

stem: A dashboard ranks teams only by volume. Team A handles 120 cases with 90% accuracy; B handles 100 with 98% accuracy. Policy requires at least 95% accuracy, then maximizes volume among qualifying teams. Which ranking follows?

choices.text: A ranks first because 108 correct cases exceed B's 98.
choices.rationale: Correct-case totals do not replace the stated percentage constraint.

choices.text: The teams tie because each leads on one dimension.
choices.rationale: The policy does not give the dimensions equal votes.

choices.text: A ranks first because its volume is 20 cases higher.
choices.rationale: This ignores the minimum accuracy rule.

choices.text: B qualifies; A does not meet the accuracy requirement.
choices.rationale: The dashboard omits a dimension that acts as a binding eligibility constraint.

choices.text: Neither qualifies because neither achieves 100% accuracy.
choices.rationale: The required threshold is 95%, not 100%.

stem: An ambiguous handwritten character is read as a letter in a word and as a digit in a number. What does this illustrate?

choices.text: The reader has deliberately chosen to misreport the mark.
choices.rationale: Deliberate misreporting is not implied.

choices.text: Context contributes to perceptual interpretation.
choices.rationale: The same ambiguous input is interpreted using surrounding information.

choices.text: Context changes the physical ink on the page.
choices.rationale: The stimulus itself remains unchanged.

choices.text: Sensory input determines perception without prior knowledge.
choices.rationale: The interpretation changes with context.

choices.text: Reading words requires a forecast of future rewards.
choices.rationale: Perceptual inference need not predict decision outcomes.

stem: In a predictive-processing account, what is a prediction error?

choices.text: An observation that confirms every feature of a model
choices.rationale: Exact confirmation would generate no discrepancy on those features.

choices.text: A consciously stated plan for the next action
choices.rationale: A plan is not the mismatch itself.

choices.text: The total amount of information stored in memory
choices.rationale: Memory size is not an error signal.

choices.text: A preference for one outcome over another
choices.rationale: Preference concerns value rather than a signal mismatch.

choices.text: A discrepancy between expected and incoming signals
choices.rationale: It identifies a mismatch that can inform updating.

stem: A person sees a shape through thick fog but has a reliable prior about what normally stands there. In a precision-weighted account, how should the fog affect the current judgment?

choices.text: Make the prior physically change the object.
choices.rationale: Inference changes interpretation, not the object.

choices.text: Increase the weight on the noisy visual signal.
choices.rationale: Noise reduces rather than increases its precision.

choices.text: Make both sources necessarily equally reliable.
choices.rationale: Equal reliability is not implied by combining sources.

choices.text: Remove the need to update when visibility improves.
choices.rationale: More reliable new evidence can support a different judgment.

choices.text: Reduce the weight on the noisy visual signal.
choices.rationale: Lower sensory reliability favors relatively more weight on other information.

stem: Thirst begins to decline shortly after drinking, before the water has fully corrected the body's fluid deficit. Which account fits the chapter's discussion?

choices.text: Drinking has permanently changed the person's values.
choices.rationale: A short-term regulatory response does not establish that change.

choices.text: The fluid deficit must already have disappeared completely.
choices.rationale: The timing in the stem rules this out.

choices.text: The person has consciously calculated blood composition.
choices.rationale: Conscious calculation is unnecessary for the mechanism.

choices.text: Thirst is unrelated to the regulation of bodily needs.
choices.rationale: Anticipation is part of regulation, not evidence against it.

choices.text: Early drinking signals help anticipate the coming correction.
choices.rationale: Regulation can use predictive signals before full absorption.

stem: One perceptual model predicts that context has more influence when an image is unclear. A rival predicts the same contextual influence at both clarity levels. Which comparison best distinguishes them?

choices.text: Compare observers' confidence before and after viewing an unclear image.
choices.rationale: A confidence change alone does not distinguish the stated predictions about perception.

choices.text: Compare clear and unclear images while keeping the same context throughout.
choices.rationale: A clarity effect alone does not test the predicted interaction with context.

choices.text: Vary context at both clarity levels and compare the size of its effect.
choices.rationale: The models disagree about whether clarity changes the influence of context.

choices.text: Vary context for unclear images and test whether perception changes at all.
choices.rationale: Both models permit a context effect on unclear images.

choices.text: Compare clear and unclear images after removing contextual information from both.
choices.rationale: Removing context prevents measuring its influence at either clarity level.

stem: A supervisor expects a trainee to improve, gives her more practice and feedback, and her performance improves. What route from expectation to outcome is described?

choices.text: The trainee's improvement proves practice was unnecessary.
choices.rationale: Practice is part of the described mechanism.

choices.text: Performance improves because the forecast is publicly accurate.
choices.rationale: Accuracy is an outcome here, not the causal pathway.

choices.text: The outcome changes before any behavior changes.
choices.rationale: The sequence explicitly includes changed treatment first.

choices.text: The initial expectation merely records a fixed ability.
choices.rationale: The stem specifies a pathway through additional support.

choices.text: Changed treatment creates opportunities for learning.
choices.rationale: The expectation alters behavior toward the trainee.

stem: Participants are randomly assigned to taste the same drink under different labels. Which finding shows a difference in reported experience rather than only expectations before tasting?

choices.text: Participants recognize one label more often before the taste test.
choices.rationale: Recognition measures familiarity, not experienced pleasantness.

choices.text: Predicted enjoyment differs between groups before either tastes the drink.
choices.rationale: These ratings measure anticipated rather than experienced pleasantness.

choices.text: Participants expect the more expensive label to indicate better ingredients.
choices.rationale: This measures a belief about quality before the experience.

choices.text: Participants assign different expected calorie counts to the two labels.
choices.rationale: Expected nutritional content is distinct from how pleasant the drink tastes.

choices.text: Ratings of how pleasant the drink tasted differ between the label groups.
choices.rationale: These ratings measure reported experience; they do not isolate experience from reporting or establish a physiological change.

stem: Researchers want to estimate the effect of an encouraging label on task performance. Which comparison is strongest?

choices.text: High-performing volunteers with a label versus low performers without it.
choices.rationale: Initial performance differs between groups.

choices.text: Identical tasks and support, with only the label varied randomly.
choices.rationale: Holding other conditions fixed isolates the assigned label.

choices.text: Compare labeled believers with unlabeled nonbelievers.
choices.rationale: Selecting on belief after assignment can bias the comparison.

choices.text: Different labels paired with different amounts of coaching.
choices.rationale: Coaching confounds the label comparison.

choices.text: Performance before a label versus afterward, without a control.
choices.rationale: Practice or time could explain the change.

stem: A tutor wants an encouraging message to give a struggling student a workable route to improvement. Which message does this best?

choices.text: “You deserve credit for the time you have already devoted to this demanding subject.”
choices.rationale: Acknowledging effort does not establish whether the study method is effective.

choices.text: “Your past success suggests more natural talent than this recent score would indicate.”
choices.rationale: Ability reassurance does not supply a method for correcting the difficulty.

choices.text: “Let's practice identifying problem types, then use feedback to choose the next exercise.”
choices.rationale: This connects a controllable strategy with feedback for improvement.

choices.text: “Your confidence may grow once you stop comparing yourself with the strongest students.”
choices.rationale: This addresses comparison without identifying a learning strategy.

choices.text: “This assessment was unusually difficult, so your score is less worrying than it seems.”
choices.rationale: Reinterpreting the score offers reassurance without a route to skill improvement.

stem: A bank predicts default, withdraws credit, and observes defaults. To estimate withdrawal's causal contribution among comparable eligible customers, which feasible and permissible study is strongest?

choices.text: Compare default rates before and after the withdrawal policy.
choices.rationale: Time trends and changing customers can confound this comparison.

choices.text: Match withdrawn customers to retained customers on recorded income alone.
choices.rationale: Unmeasured or unmatched risk differences can remain.

choices.text: Refit the default model using only withdrawn customers.
choices.rationale: Recalibration within one action does not estimate the counterfactual effect.

choices.text: Compare high-risk withdrawn customers with low-risk retained customers.
choices.rationale: Risk and treatment are deliberately confounded.

choices.text: Randomly assign credit retention or withdrawal and compare defaults.
choices.rationale: Randomization separates the action's effect from customers' initial risk.

stem: Which statement distinguishes a utility representation from a psychological account of valuation?

choices.text: Utility requires monetary outcomes; valuation permits nonmonetary outcomes.
choices.rationale: Utility can represent preferences over nonmonetary consequences.

choices.text: Utility represents preference ordering; valuation explains how appeal arises.
choices.rationale: Representation and psychological explanation address different tasks.

choices.text: Utility describes correct choices; valuation describes departures from rationality.
choices.rationale: Valuation also contributes to choices consistent with a rational benchmark.

choices.text: Utility measures experienced pleasure; valuation measures willingness to pay.
choices.rationale: Utility need not measure pleasure, and valuation is broader than monetary bids.

choices.text: Utility and valuation are interchangeable accounts of how preferences form.
choices.rationale: A representation of rankings does not itself explain their formation.

stem: A person dislikes a job applicant more after an unrelated stressful commute. Which influence is most directly illustrated?

choices.text: A sunk cost of employing the applicant
choices.rationale: Employment costs have not been incurred.

choices.text: Bayesian updating from new work evidence
choices.rationale: The commute supplies no relevant work evidence.

choices.text: A change in the applicant's formal credentials
choices.rationale: The applicant's credentials did not change.

choices.text: Integral concern about the applicant's qualifications
choices.rationale: No qualification-related concern caused the feeling.

choices.text: Incidental emotion spilling into evaluation
choices.rationale: The source of the emotion is outside the applicant evaluation.

stem: A retailer cuts the price of an unfamiliar wine. Which response could offset the benefit of its lower purchase cost?

choices.text: Buyers can afford more bottles with the same total expenditure.
choices.rationale: Increased purchasing power reinforces the benefit of the lower price.

choices.text: Buyers see less money at risk if they dislike the wine.
choices.rationale: A smaller financial downside makes trying the wine more attractive.

choices.text: Buyers find that a bottle now fits within their spending budget.
choices.rationale: Relaxing a budget constraint supports rather than offsets purchase.

choices.text: Buyers judge the saving relative to the old price more favorably.
choices.rationale: A more attractive saving reinforces the price cut's appeal.

choices.text: Buyers revise their estimate of the wine's quality downward.
choices.rationale: Price can serve as a quality signal as well as a cost.

stem: After a large lunch, a person values an additional sandwich less than before lunch. Which explanation is closest to the chapter's account?

choices.text: The sandwich has become a sunk cost.
choices.rationale: Being less desirable does not make an object a sunk expenditure.

choices.text: Current bodily needs alter the sandwich's subjective value.
choices.rationale: Valuation depends partly on the person's current state.

choices.text: The change is evidence of an incorrect probability calculation.
choices.rationale: The comparison need not involve probability calculation.

choices.text: The person's long-run goals must have reversed.
choices.rationale: Temporary satiety need not reverse long-run goals.

choices.text: The sandwich's monetary price must have fallen.
choices.rationale: No price change is required.

stem: Neural activity recorded while people hear music predicts their later bids. Which additional finding best distinguishes a causal contribution of the measured region from a predictive association?

choices.text: The association recurs in a larger group of listeners from the same population.
choices.rationale: Replication strengthens an association without identifying its cause.

choices.text: A targeted neural intervention changes bids with relevant alternative explanations controlled.
choices.rationale: An intervention tests the consequences of changing the neural process.

choices.text: The signal correlates with both bids and reported liking for the music.
choices.rationale: Converging correlations do not establish a causal contribution.

choices.text: The signal predicts bids in listeners excluded from fitting the prediction model.
choices.rationale: Held-out prediction tests generalization rather than causation.

choices.text: A more flexible model fits the originally observed bids more accurately.
choices.rationale: Better fit does not show what happens when the neural process is changed.

stem: After a covert swap, a participant explains why she preferred the picture she actually rejected. What is the main lesson?

choices.text: A sincere reason can fail to identify what caused the choice.
choices.rationale: People can construct explanations for an outcome they did not choose.

choices.text: The experiment measures the participant's risk aversion.
choices.rationale: No risky choice is involved.

choices.text: Giving an explanation proves the swap was detected.
choices.rationale: Explanation can occur without detecting the substitution.

choices.text: The rejected picture was secretly chosen on the first trial.
choices.rationale: The stem specifies the original choice and the later swap.

choices.text: The participant must be deliberately lying about the swap.
choices.rationale: Sincere rationalization does not require deliberate deception.

stem: After freely choosing one of two similar courses, a student emphasizes the chosen course's strengths and dismisses the rejected course. Which process fits this post-choice change?

choices.text: Applying a fixed monetary exchange rate
choices.rationale: The judgment concerns attitudes, not currency.

choices.text: Reversing a conditional probability
choices.rationale: No conditional probability is being calculated.

choices.text: Updating from a new course grade
choices.rationale: No grade or new performance evidence is supplied.

choices.text: Detecting a change in the course descriptions
choices.rationale: The stem specifies a change in evaluation, not course information.

choices.text: Reducing cognitive dissonance
choices.rationale: Re-evaluation makes the completed choice easier to justify.

stem: A committee rewrites its reasons after learning a project's result. Which practice most directly supports later learning about the original reasoning?

choices.text: Remove forecasts from the evaluation discussion.
choices.rationale: Without forecasts, prediction quality cannot be assessed.

choices.text: Date the forecast, assumptions, and reasons before acting.
choices.rationale: A contemporaneous record separates prior beliefs from later explanations.

choices.text: Write the minutes after the final outcome is known.
choices.rationale: This permits the same retrospective reconstruction.

choices.text: Ask only the most confident member to recall the meeting.
choices.rationale: Confidence does not preserve an unbiased record.

choices.text: Judge the process solely by whether the project succeeded.
choices.rationale: Outcome alone mixes decision quality with luck.

stem: A firm calls every success evidence of its strategy and every failure an exceptional external shock. Which change most directly makes the strategy testable?

choices.text: Publish a longer narrative after each successful project.
choices.rationale: Additional supportive narrative does not make failure informative.

choices.text: Replace recorded results with employees' recollections.
choices.rationale: This weakens rather than strengthens the evidence.

choices.text: Specify in advance which outcomes would count against it.
choices.rationale: A test needs possible evidence that could challenge the claim.

choices.text: Ask executives to state their confidence more forcefully.
choices.rationale: Confidence is not a disconfirmation rule.

choices.text: Exclude external shocks only after seeing the outcome.
choices.rationale: Post hoc exclusions can protect the claim from challenge.

stem: A panel says experience drove its hiring choice. Records contain applicants' experience, initial ratings of speaking polish, and rankings made before discussion. Which analysis best tests that explanation against a polish-based rival?

choices.text: Count references to experience in the final justification.
choices.rationale: Repeated stated reasons do not establish the causes of the ranking.

choices.text: Compare polish with current recollections of initial rankings.
choices.rationale: Available dated rankings are preferable to reconstructed memory.

choices.text: Compare experience only among the selected applicants.
choices.rationale: Selection removes informative rejected cases and ignores the rival cue.

choices.text: Ask panelists now to rate how much they valued experience.
choices.rationale: Retrospective reports may reproduce the justification being tested.

choices.text: Compare both experience and polish with the recorded initial rankings.
choices.rationale: Contemporaneous measures permit comparison of the two proposed influences.

stem: A club overlooks renting equipment, exaggerates the durability of buying, and never decides how much storage space matters. Which sequence names these three problems?

choices.text: Valuation, prediction, implementation
choices.rationale: The first is omission of an option; the third is weighting a consequence.

choices.text: Implementation, learning, prediction
choices.rationale: The problems arise before implementation or outcome feedback.

choices.text: Learning, option construction, valuation
choices.rationale: The first problem is not learning from an outcome.

choices.text: Prediction, valuation, option construction
choices.rationale: This shifts each problem to the wrong stage.

choices.text: Option construction, prediction, valuation
choices.rationale: The problems concern alternatives, consequences, and their importance respectively.

stem: A family tradition makes a meal feel especially valuable to one person. Which conclusion distinguishes explanation from normative evaluation?

choices.text: An inherited tradition determines the ethically best meal for everyone.
choices.rationale: Origins do not establish universal moral worth.

choices.text: A meal has value only through its market price.
choices.rationale: Valuation also reflects identity, relationships, and experience.

choices.text: A culturally learned value cannot influence a real preference.
choices.rationale: Learned meanings can shape subjective value.

choices.text: The tradition helps explain the value; it does not settle what everyone ought to choose.
choices.rationale: Socially acquired meaning explains preferences without supplying a universal prescription.

choices.text: A utility representation must ignore the meal's social meaning.
choices.rationale: Preference ordering can reflect consequences with social meaning.

stem: A job comparison page makes salary prominent and hides commuting time. Applicants focus on salary. Which redesign best addresses the resulting comparison problem?

choices.text: Explain the selected job only after the contract is signed.
choices.rationale: Later justification does not repair the original comparison.

choices.text: Ask applicants to ignore their personal travel preferences.
choices.rationale: Preferences over commuting remain relevant.

choices.text: Increase the prominence of the highest salary further.
choices.rationale: This intensifies the original attentional imbalance.

choices.text: Show salary and commuting time together on clearly labeled scales.
choices.rationale: Making both consequences interpretable helps them enter valuation.

choices.text: Remove salary so that commuting becomes the only visible attribute.
choices.rationale: That replaces one incomplete comparison with another.

stem: A supplier recommendation reverses when an uncertain failure rate rises from 3% to 4%, both plausible values. Which response uses sensitivity analysis appropriately?

choices.text: Average the suppliers' projected costs and select the quote closest to that average.
choices.rationale: Closeness to an average does not test the uncertain input that changes the ranking.

choices.text: Replace the failure rate with 3.5% and treat the resulting recommendation as settled.
choices.rationale: A midpoint estimate hides the recommendation's dependence on the uncertain input.

choices.text: Compare outcomes across that range and locate where the preferred supplier changes.
choices.rationale: Sensitivity analysis examines how plausible input changes affect the recommendation.

choices.text: Apply the larger failure estimate to every supplier without comparing their evidence.
choices.rationale: Uniform pessimism does not identify the effect of each consequential uncertainty.

choices.text: Report projected costs to more decimal places while retaining the original failure estimate.
choices.rationale: More displayed precision does not address sensitivity to the uncertain input.

stem: A coach predicts an athlete will excel and gives that athlete extra practice. Later success is treated as proof that the coach merely recognized innate ability. What has been overlooked?

choices.text: The prediction may have altered the athlete's learning environment.
choices.rationale: Treatment induced by a forecast can help cause the outcome.

choices.text: The prediction must have been consciously insincere.
choices.rationale: The coach can sincerely believe the forecast.

choices.text: A correct forecast rules out effects of the coach's actions.
choices.rationale: Predictive success and causal influence can coexist.

choices.text: Practice cannot be measured as part of a causal pathway.
choices.rationale: Practice is precisely a potentially measurable mediator.

choices.text: The outcome supplies a direct measure of innate ability alone.
choices.rationale: Changed opportunities prevent that simple interpretation.

stem: Customers give higher ratings to coffee sold at higher prices, but both the coffees and customers differ. Which follow-up best separates a price-induced expectation effect from a physical coffee difference?

choices.text: Compare premium beans with cheaper beans at their usual prices.
choices.rationale: Physical quality and price then vary together.

choices.text: Replace tasting ratings with the retailer's preferred price.
choices.rationale: A preferred price does not measure the experience under study.

choices.text: Randomly assign price labels to tasters served the same coffee.
choices.rationale: Identical coffee and random labels isolate the label manipulation.

choices.text: Change both the price and serving temperature.
choices.rationale: Temperature becomes an additional explanation.

choices.text: Ask only participants who already prefer expensive coffee.
choices.rationale: Selection limits the comparison and does not isolate the manipulation.

stem: A person recognizes a blurred face using context, then forecasts that the recognized person will accept an invitation. Later she explains why she had expected acceptance. Which distinction best organizes the sequence?

choices.text: An action, an outcome, then a controlled experiment
choices.rationale: No controlled manipulation is described.

choices.text: Perceptual inference, consequence forecast, then retrospective explanation
choices.rationale: The stages answer what is present, what will happen, and why a prior judgment was made.

choices.text: A consequence forecast followed by two perceptual inferences
choices.rationale: Recognition comes first, and the final account concerns a prior judgment.

choices.text: Three direct recordings of external reality
choices.rationale: Inference, forecasting, and explanation all involve interpretation.

choices.text: Three judgments of the invitation's monetary value
choices.rationale: None is necessarily a valuation in money.

stem: A job seeker initially compares salary alone. She then discovers that one employer will trade a little salary for flexible hours, which she values highly. What should she do next?

choices.text: Choose the higher salary because only money is comparable.
choices.rationale: Nonmonetary consequences can be valued and compared.

choices.text: Assume flexibility has the same value for every applicant.
choices.rationale: The chapter emphasizes differences in subjective value.

choices.text: Infer that the employer's first offer was irrational.
choices.rationale: Negotiability does not establish irrationality.

choices.text: Evaluate the newly feasible salary–hours package against alternatives.
choices.rationale: Option construction and valuation should incorporate the negotiable trade-off.

choices.text: Treat the original salary as a cost already paid.
choices.rationale: An offer is not an incurred sunk cost.

stem: An expected-profit maximizer can take a certain €50 or launch a product earning €120 on success and €0 otherwise; success has probability 0.4. Perfect information costs €15 and arrives before the choice; both actions remain available. What policy maximizes expected net profit?

choices.text: Buy information; launch only on success, otherwise take €50.
choices.rationale: Perfect information yields 0.4×120 + 0.6×50 − 15 = €63, above €50.

choices.text: Decline information and launch the product.
choices.rationale: Its expected profit is €48, below the certain €50.

choices.text: Buy information and launch regardless of its result.
choices.rationale: This earns €48 − €15 = €33 in expectation.

choices.text: Buy information and take €50 regardless of its result.
choices.rationale: This earns €35 and wastes the information.

choices.text: Decline information and take €50.
choices.rationale: This misses the available €63 expected net payoff.

stem: An encouraging label increases reported task enjoyment. Participants say it helped them concentrate. Which follow-up most directly tests this proposed mechanism?

choices.text: Test whether the label increases task performance in a larger randomized comparison.
choices.rationale: An additional outcome does not isolate the proposed concentration pathway.

choices.text: Ask participants to predict which label would help concentration before completing the task.
choices.rationale: Beliefs about a mechanism do not establish that it caused the outcome.

choices.text: Repeat the label comparison with more participants and more detailed explanations afterward.
choices.rationale: Greater precision and fuller introspection do not independently test the proposed mediator.

choices.text: Compare enjoyment among participants who later say the label helped them concentrate.
choices.rationale: Selecting on retrospective explanations can confound the proposed mediator with the outcome.

choices.text: Vary the label and a separate concentration intervention, measuring concentration and enjoyment.
choices.rationale: Testing both links provides stronger mechanism evidence, provided the intervention's other effects are addressed.

stem: What does the System 1–System 2 distinction describe in this book?

choices.text: Contrasting modes of processing, not two separate brain organs
choices.rationale: The framework distinguishes automatic from effortful processing.

choices.text: Conscious preferences versus unconscious preferences only
choices.rationale: The distinction concerns processing, not just preference awareness.

choices.text: Two anatomical regions with exclusive responsibility for choice
choices.rationale: The framework is not a literal anatomical division.

choices.text: Unlearned reflexes versus everything acquired through practice
choices.rationale: Skilled automatic responses can be learned.

choices.text: Emotional errors followed by invariably correct reasoning
choices.rationale: Emotion can inform judgment, and deliberation can err.

stem: Asked whether a candidate can manage complex projects, an interviewer answers by judging how confidently the candidate speaks. What substitution has occurred?

choices.text: Speaking confidence is used as a cue for managerial competence.
choices.rationale: An easier impression stands in for the target judgment.

choices.text: A base rate is updated using independently verified work records.
choices.rationale: Neither base rates nor verified records appear in the stem.

choices.text: A remembered outcome replaces a recorded prior forecast.
choices.rationale: This would concern hindsight, not the stated substitution.

choices.text: Project complexity is used as a cue for speaking confidence.
choices.rationale: This reverses the target and the cue.

choices.text: A salary figure anchors an estimate of project costs.
choices.rationale: No numerical anchor is supplied.

stem: Which setting offers the strongest basis for trusting practiced intuition?

choices.text: Repeated decisions with stable cues and timely, diagnostic feedback
choices.rationale: These conditions support learning useful regularities.

choices.text: Novel problems judged by agreement among equally inexperienced peers
choices.rationale: Agreement is not experience with diagnostic outcomes.

choices.text: Rapidly changing rules with repeated but delayed vague feedback
choices.rationale: Changing rules and weak feedback impair calibration.

choices.text: One-off decisions with vivid stories and little outcome feedback
choices.rationale: Vividness cannot substitute for learning valid cues.

choices.text: High confidence acquired through years without checking outcomes
choices.rationale: Time and confidence alone do not demonstrate valid learning.

stem: An analyst notices low confidence in a forecast and then consults a reference class. Which part of the sequence is metacognitive control?

choices.text: Having the eventual forecast turn out correctly
choices.rationale: The outcome is distinct from regulating the reasoning process.

choices.text: Producing the first estimate before reflection
choices.rationale: This is the initial judgment being monitored.

choices.text: Choosing to consult the reference class
choices.rationale: Control selects an action in response to a monitored state.

choices.text: Noticing the low confidence
choices.rationale: This is monitoring rather than the subsequent control decision.

choices.text: Experiencing the initial feeling of uncertainty
choices.rationale: The feeling is information to monitor, not the checking action.

stem: A pen and notebook cost €4.40 together. The notebook costs €4.00 more than the pen. Which check correctly evaluates the tempting answer that the pen costs €0.40?

choices.text: It implies a €4.60 total; the pen should cost €0.30.
choices.rationale: Both the implied total and the proposed solution are wrong.

choices.text: It implies a €4.80 total; the pen should cost €0.10.
choices.rationale: The rejection is right, but €0.10 gives only €4.20 total.

choices.text: It implies a €4.40 total; the pen should cost €0.40.
choices.rationale: This treats the difference as the notebook's price.

choices.text: It implies a €4.80 total; the pen should cost €0.20.
choices.rationale: With a €0.40 pen, the notebook is €4.40; solving 2p + 4 = 4.40 gives €0.20.

choices.text: It implies a €4.00 total; the pen should cost €0.40.
choices.rationale: The two prices under that guess sum to €4.80.

stem: Repeated reports of the same old lift accidents make examples easier to recall. Lina treats that ease as evidence that accidents have become more frequent. Which heuristic is most directly implicated?

choices.text: Endowment
choices.rationale: Ownership is not affecting valuation.

choices.text: Availability
choices.rationale: Ease of recalling examples substitutes for frequency evidence.

choices.text: Sunk-cost reasoning
choices.rationale: Past expenditure does not drive the estimate.

choices.text: Representativeness
choices.rationale: No match to a category prototype is specified.

choices.text: Anchoring
choices.rationale: No initial numerical value is supplied.

stem: A manager's enthusiasm for a new technology leads her to rate both its benefits as high and its risks as low, without separate evidence for either rating. Which heuristic fits best?

choices.text: Availability
choices.rationale: The stem emphasizes feeling rather than ease of recall.

choices.text: Affect
choices.rationale: A global positive feeling shapes both assessments.

choices.text: Mental accounting
choices.rationale: No labeled budget separates funds.

choices.text: Regression to the mean
choices.rationale: No extreme repeated measurement is involved.

choices.text: Representativeness
choices.rationale: No resemblance to a category is doing the work.

stem: A quiet, bookish person is judged more likely to be an archivist than a sales worker. Which finding most directly challenges reliance on that resemblance?

choices.text: Quiet, bookish sales workers greatly outnumber quiet, bookish archivists in the relevant population.
choices.rationale: The relevant frequencies can outweigh a stereotypical match.

choices.text: The description is presented in the same wording to everyone making the judgment.
choices.rationale: Standardized wording does not make resemblance sufficient evidence.

choices.text: The person prefers the working conditions associated with archives to those in sales.
choices.rationale: Preferred working conditions do not establish the person's current occupation.

choices.text: Respondents agree closely about which occupation best fits the description they read.
choices.rationale: Consensus about fit does not supply the relevant population frequencies.

choices.text: Archivists receive higher personality-match ratings than sales workers from the same judges.
choices.rationale: Agreement about resemblance does not establish occupational probability.

stem: Three news sites report that a factory will close. All cite the same agency dispatch. Which additional finding most increases their value as independent evidence?

choices.text: Each site gave the story a prominent place on its main page.
choices.rationale: Prominence affects visibility rather than evidential independence.

choices.text: Each site published the account at a different time of day.
choices.rationale: Timing does not separate the reports' informational origin.

choices.text: Each site attracted comments from readers who believed the account.
choices.rationale: Reader reactions need not provide independent knowledge of the closure.

choices.text: Each site paraphrased the dispatch using different headlines and wording.
choices.rationale: Different wording does not create a new underlying source.

choices.text: Each site also verified the closure with a different firsthand source.
choices.rationale: Separate corroboration adds evidence beyond the shared dispatch.

stem: During the same period, risk A produces 20 incidents in 200 exposures, and B produces 30 in 3,000. Incident severity and prevention costs differ but have not been evaluated. Which conclusion is warranted?

choices.text: B must have the larger expected loss per exposure because it has more incidents.
choices.rationale: Expected loss also depends on the denominator and severity.

choices.text: A must receive all prevention funding because its rate is ten times higher.
choices.rationale: Severity, intervention effects, and costs remain relevant.

choices.text: B has the higher incident rate because its total incident count is larger.
choices.rationale: Counts must be related to exposure denominators.

choices.text: Equal observation periods imply equal incident rates for the two risks.
choices.rationale: Exposure counts and incident fractions differ.

choices.text: A has the higher incident rate; prevention priorities need consequence and cost information too.
choices.rationale: Rates are 10% and 1%; frequency alone does not determine the best intervention.

stem: A product team interviews only satisfied users when testing its belief that customers like a new design. Which process is most directly shown?

choices.text: Selective search for confirming evidence
choices.rationale: The sampling rule privileges evidence favorable to the belief.

choices.text: Changing customers' experience through an expectation
choices.rationale: The stem describes evidence selection, not altered experience.

choices.text: Regression toward average satisfaction
choices.rationale: No repeated extreme measurement is described.

choices.text: Weighting losses more than equivalent gains
choices.rationale: No gain–loss asymmetry is specified.

choices.text: Updating from a representative customer sample
choices.rationale: Dissatisfied customers are excluded.

stem: A salesperson attributes a strong month to skill and a weak month to unlucky customers, without checking either explanation. Which label fits this asymmetric account?

choices.text: A descriptive social norm
choices.rationale: This is an explanation of performance, not others' prevalence of behavior.

choices.text: An unbiased comparison of rival causes
choices.rationale: The favorable asymmetry is precisely what requires examination.

choices.text: Base-rate updating
choices.rationale: No relevant frequency evidence is being incorporated.

choices.text: A fixed reference-class forecast
choices.rationale: The account is retrospective and outcome dependent.

choices.text: Self-serving attribution
choices.rationale: Success and failure receive explanations that protect the self.

stem: An employee follows a script imposed by management. A customer concludes that the employee has a rigid personality. Which comparison best tests that inference?

choices.text: Observe another employee following the same required script with that customer.
choices.rationale: Shared scripted behavior does not reveal the first employee's disposition.

choices.text: Ask managers whether they described the employee as dependable when hiring.
choices.rationale: A hiring description does not directly test the inference of personal rigidity.

choices.text: Compare how accurately the employee follows different required scripts.
choices.rationale: This still observes behavior under imposed rules.

choices.text: Ask the customer to rate the employee again after the same encounter.
choices.rationale: Repeating the judgment adds no behavior outside the constraint.

choices.text: Observe the employee handling a similar request when allowed discretion.
choices.rationale: Behavior without the constraint helps distinguish disposition from the imposed script.

stem: A team thinks a service succeeds only when response time is under one hour. Which observation would most directly challenge that claim?

choices.text: A successful case with a response time below one hour
choices.rationale: This is consistent with the claim.

choices.text: An unsuccessful case with a response time above one hour
choices.rationale: Failure without the condition is also consistent with necessity.

choices.text: Several rapid responses whose outcomes were not recorded
choices.rationale: Without outcomes, these cases cannot test necessity.

choices.text: A successful case with a response time above one hour
choices.rationale: Success without the purported necessary condition refutes necessity.

choices.text: The team's preference for rapid responses
choices.rationale: Preference is not a test of the empirical claim.

stem: Rival policy groups accept weak favorable evidence but demand strong unfavorable evidence. Which procedure most directly constrains that asymmetry before new results are seen?

choices.text: Select equal numbers of studies favoring each policy.
choices.rationale: Equal counts do not ensure equal evidential quality.

choices.text: Let each side independently select only its preferred studies.
choices.rationale: Separate selective searches can retain the asymmetry.

choices.text: Precommit to common inclusion rules and quality criteria.
choices.rationale: The same standards can then be applied regardless of which policy benefits.

choices.text: Average the confidence ratings of both advocacy teams.
choices.rationale: Balanced confidence does not assess study quality.

choices.text: Blind policy names but allow criteria to change after results.
choices.rationale: Post-result rule changes can preserve motivated evaluation.

stem: An arbitrary example price of €900 is shown before people estimate an item's value; estimates are higher than after a €300 example. Which effect is illustrated?

choices.text: Anchoring
choices.rationale: A starting number pulls subsequent estimates toward it.

choices.text: Present bias
choices.rationale: The comparison does not involve timing.

choices.text: Availability
choices.rationale: No recall-frequency judgment is involved.

choices.text: Choice blindness
choices.rationale: No selected item has been covertly substituted.

choices.text: Endowment
choices.rationale: No ownership difference is specified.

stem: A polished presentation leads evaluators to rate the speaker highly on technical accuracy without checking the analysis. What is the closest account?

choices.text: A decoy introduced into the choice set
choices.rationale: No third option is added.

choices.text: A sunk-cost response to prior training
choices.rationale: Past investment is not the source of the judgment.

choices.text: A descriptive norm about technical accuracy
choices.rationale: The prevalence of others' behavior is not specified.

choices.text: A Bayesian update from audited calculations
choices.rationale: The calculations have not been checked.

choices.text: A halo from presentation quality
choices.rationale: A favorable dimension spills into a distinct judgment.

stem: Laptops differ only in price and battery life; lower price and longer life are preferred. A costs €700 with 8 hours, B €900 with 12 hours, and C €900 with 10 hours. Which option asymmetrically dominates C?

choices.text: Neither A nor B
choices.rationale: B is better on battery life with no price disadvantage.

choices.text: Both A and B
choices.rationale: Only B is at least as good on both attributes.

choices.text: B only
choices.rationale: B has the same price and longer life; A is cheaper but has shorter life.

choices.text: A only
choices.rationale: A trades a lower price for shorter battery life.

choices.text: C dominates both A and B
choices.rationale: C is worse than B on battery life and costs more than A.

stem: People evaluating a single dictionary struggle to judge whether 12,000 entries is many. Side-by-side comparison with a 20,000-entry dictionary makes the difference matter more. Which concept is central?

choices.text: Reciprocal cooperation
choices.rationale: No response to another person's kindness is involved.

choices.text: Regression to the mean
choices.rationale: No extreme repeated outcome is being explained.

choices.text: Present bias
choices.rationale: There is no immediate-versus-delayed trade-off.

choices.text: Evaluability
choices.rationale: Comparison makes an otherwise hard-to-interpret attribute easier to assess.

choices.text: Loss aversion
choices.rationale: No ownership or loss relative to a reference point is necessary.

stem: An analyst adjusts one program's cost until she judges two safety programs equally attractive. Later, with the same information and consequences, she reports strictly preferring the safer program when directly comparing them. Which interpretation best fits the prominence hypothesis?

choices.text: Matching and direct choice reveal the same strict ordering.
choices.rationale: Indifference in matching differs from the later stated strict preference.

choices.text: Safety receives greater weight in direct choice than in matching.
choices.rationale: The response task can alter the weight of a prominent attribute despite unchanged consequences.

choices.text: A third dominated program changed the two-option comparison.
choices.rationale: No third option was introduced.

choices.text: The later preference establishes that the safety probabilities changed.
choices.rationale: The stem holds the information and consequences constant.

choices.text: The program's safety advantage must have had zero weight during matching.
choices.rationale: A change in relative weight does not imply the earlier weight was zero.

stem: One report says 92 of 100 machines pass inspection; another says 8 of 100 fail the same inspection. What is held constant?

choices.text: The words used to describe performance
choices.rationale: The descriptions deliberately differ.

choices.text: The underlying inspection outcomes
choices.rationale: Passing and failing are complementary descriptions of the same results.

choices.text: The salience of machine failures
choices.rationale: The failure frame makes failures more explicit.

choices.text: The evaluator's final recommendation
choices.rationale: Equivalent facts need not produce the same recommendation.

choices.text: The emotional response to the report
choices.rationale: Framing can alter this response.

stem: A survey asks, “How much should the council increase parking fees?” before establishing whether an increase is wanted. What assumption is embedded in the question?

choices.text: That some increase is the relevant action
choices.rationale: The question directs attention to the amount rather than whether to increase.

choices.text: That a decrease would be legally prohibited
choices.rationale: The wording provides no legal information.

choices.text: That current fees equal zero
choices.rationale: No current fee is specified.

choices.text: That the council has already collected the extra revenue
choices.rationale: The question concerns a possible future change.

choices.text: That all residents use council parking
choices.rationale: Use by all residents is not presupposed.

stem: Among completed journeys, a safety brochure gives only the percentage with no injury. Which revision best implements complementary framing?

choices.text: Add the injury percentage for the same population and period.
choices.rationale: Complementary outcomes expose the same facts from both sides.

choices.text: Show only the number of passengers who bought tickets.
choices.rationale: Ticket purchases do not describe the injury outcome.

choices.text: Replace the statistic with a vivid successful journey.
choices.rationale: A story does not supply the missing complement.

choices.text: Add an injury count drawn from a different year.
choices.rationale: Changing the period prevents a clean complementary comparison.

choices.text: Use larger type for the current statistic.
choices.rationale: Prominence leaves the one-sided frame unchanged.

stem: A form changes “10% service failures” to “90% service success.” Which feature was directly changed?

choices.text: The objective success rate
choices.rationale: Both descriptions state the same rate.

choices.text: The descriptive frame
choices.rationale: The wording changes the presented complement.

choices.text: The default option
choices.rationale: Changing this wording does not select a different option.

choices.text: The financial incentive
choices.rationale: No payoff change is specified.

choices.text: The feasible set
choices.rationale: No option is added or removed.

stem: Over one year, an intervention reduces event risk from 2 per 1,000 to 1 per 1,000. Which description preserves both the baseline and the absolute and relative changes?

choices.text: From 2 to 1 per 1,000: one fewer event, a 50% relative reduction.
choices.rationale: The change is 1/1,000, or half the original risk.

choices.text: From 2 to 1 per 1,000: one fewer event, a 1% relative reduction.
choices.rationale: Relative reduction divides the change by the baseline two.

choices.text: From 2 to 1 per 1,000: one percentage point, a 50% relative reduction.
choices.rationale: One per 1,000 is 0.1 percentage points, not one point.

choices.text: From 2 to 1 per 100: one fewer event, a 50% relative reduction.
choices.rationale: This changes the denominator and therefore the risks.

choices.text: From 2 to 0 per 1,000: two fewer events, a 50% relative reduction.
choices.rationale: This changes the final risk and would imply a 100% reduction.

stem: After reading several words about kitchens, a reader resolves an ambiguous word toward its cooking-related meaning. Which process is most directly illustrated?

choices.text: Loss aversion
choices.rationale: No gain–loss comparison is involved.

choices.text: Semantic priming
choices.rationale: Related concepts have become more accessible.

choices.text: A sunk-cost effect
choices.rationale: No past expense drives the interpretation.

choices.text: An endowment effect
choices.rationale: Ownership is not manipulated.

choices.text: A default effect
choices.rationale: No option is preselected.

stem: A repeated claim feels more credible even though each repetition traces to the same unsupported source. Which phenomenon fits best?

choices.text: Regression to average accuracy
choices.rationale: No repeated noisy measurement of accuracy is described.

choices.text: A change in the claim's logical content
choices.rationale: The claim is repeated, not revised.

choices.text: The illusory-truth effect
choices.rationale: Familiarity can raise perceived truth without new evidence.

choices.text: Loss aversion from abandoning a possession
choices.rationale: Neither possession nor a monetary loss is specified.

choices.text: Bayesian learning from independent confirmations
choices.rationale: The repetitions are not independent confirmations.

stem: A designer makes instructions easier to read. Which comparison best tests whether the revision improves understanding?

choices.text: Randomly assign the versions and compare confidence in having understood them.
choices.rationale: Fluency can raise confidence without improving comprehension.

choices.text: Randomly assign the versions and compare performance on new examples.
choices.rationale: Transfer to new examples tests application beyond perceived ease.

choices.text: Randomly assign the versions and compare ratings of clarity and visual appeal.
choices.rationale: Perceived clarity and appeal need not improve application.

choices.text: Randomly assign the versions and compare how quickly readers finish the page.
choices.rationale: Reading speed does not establish correct understanding.

choices.text: Randomly assign the versions and compare recognition of phrases from the instructions.
choices.rationale: Recognizing wording does not establish understanding of its meaning.

stem: Two unfamiliar logos receive similar initial liking ratings. One then appears repeatedly on unrelated screens. Which later result best fits the mere-exposure effect?

choices.text: The repeated logo is recognized more accurately but receives unchanged liking ratings.
choices.rationale: Recognition alone does not demonstrate an increase in liking.

choices.text: The unseen logo receives higher ratings because participants prefer novel designs.
choices.rationale: This describes a novelty preference rather than mere exposure.

choices.text: Both logos receive higher ratings after evidence of better product performance.
choices.rationale: This change follows new product information rather than repeated exposure.

choices.text: The repeated logo receives higher liking ratings without new product information.
choices.rationale: Repeated exposure can increase liking without providing evidence of better performance.

choices.text: Both logos retain equal ratings because their products have identical attributes.
choices.rationale: The mere-exposure prediction permits familiarity to affect liking despite equal attributes.

stem: One study finds better recall when retrieval mood matches learning mood. Another finds sad participants preferentially recall unpleasant events regardless of learning mood. Which pair describes these patterns?

choices.text: Mood-dependent memory in both studies
choices.rationale: The second does not require matching the mood at learning.

choices.rationale: The first matches states across learning and retrieval; the second matches content to current mood.

choices.text: Mood-congruent memory in both studies
choices.rationale: The first concerns matching states, not the emotional content recalled.

choices.text: Mood-congruent memory; mood-dependent memory
choices.rationale: This reverses the state-matching and content-matching mechanisms.

choices.text: Semantic priming; mere exposure
choices.rationale: These do not capture the two specified mood relationships.

stem: A classifier flags 80% of defective items. Which probability does this statement give?

choices.rationale: This is the base rate, not the detection rate.

choices.text: P(defective given flagged)
choices.rationale: This reverses the conditional.

choices.text: P(flagged given defective)
choices.rationale: The denominator is defective items.

choices.text: P(flagged given sound)
choices.rationale: This is the false-positive rate.

choices.text: P(sound given unflagged)
choices.rationale: This is a different inverse conditional.

choices.rationale: That sum generally double-counts the intersection.

choices.text: P(A and B) equals P(A given B).
choices.rationale: Conditional probability uses a different denominator.

choices.text: P(A and B) is no greater than P(A).
choices.rationale: The intersection is a subset of A.

choices.text: P(A and B) equals 1 − P(A).
choices.rationale: That expression gives the complement of A.

choices.text: P(A and B) is greater than P(A).
choices.rationale: A subset cannot have greater probability than its containing event.

The intersection should be subtracted, not added.

choices.rationale: These are the prior rates before using the screen.

choices.text: 90% in both groups
choices.rationale: Sensitivity is not the probability of a defect given a positive screen.

choices.text: 50% in A and 50% in B
choices.rationale: Equal test performance does not erase different priors.

choices.text: 90% in A and 50% in B
choices.rationale: This reverses the correctly calculated posterior rates.

choices.text: 50% in A and 90% in B

stem: A fair coin has landed heads four times. What is the probability of heads on the next toss?

choices.rationale: This is the probability of four specified heads in advance.
In the usual fair-coin model, tosses are independent, so the previous heads do not change the next-toss probability of 1/2.
This is the probability of five specified heads in advance.
Four previous heads do not make the next toss 80% likely.
Past heads do not create a balancing requirement.

stem: A forecaster's stated 90% intervals contain the true value in only 55% of many comparable cases. Which error is most directly evident?

choices.text: Hindsight bias
choices.rationale: The intervals were stated before outcomes occurred.

choices.text: Overplacement
choices.rationale: Relative rank compared with other people is not measured.

choices.text: Loss aversion
choices.rationale: No asymmetry between gains and losses is specified.

choices.text: Overestimation of average outcomes
choices.rationale: Undercoverage need not imply a directional bias in means.

choices.text: Overprecision
choices.rationale: Achieved coverage is substantially below the stated confidence.

stem: A coach praises players after unusually strong performances and criticizes them after unusually weak ones. With stable ability and independent mean-zero performance fluctuations, which average pattern is expected across many comparable cases if neither response has an effect?

choices.text: Random performance variation disappears in the next match.
choices.rationale: Noise remains even when conditional averages regress.

choices.text: Every player's performance becomes identical.
choices.rationale: Regression does not eliminate stable ability differences.

choices.text: Performance rises after both praise and criticism.
choices.rationale: Regression predicts different directions from the two extremes.

choices.text: Performance falls after praise and rises after criticism.
choices.rationale: Selection on extremes creates regression toward typical performance.

choices.text: Performance falls after both praise and criticism.
choices.rationale: Weak extreme performances tend to rise, not fall further.

stem: A team forecasts two months for a project by imagining a smooth sequence of tasks. Similar completed projects usually took five months. What is the most useful next step?

choices.text: Ignore the completed projects because every project differs.
choices.rationale: Relevant differences justify adjustments, not blanket rejection.

choices.text: Start from the comparison projects and justify specific adjustments.
choices.rationale: The outside view disciplines the inside narrative with observed outcomes.

choices.text: Report two months with more decimal places.
choices.rationale: Numerical precision does not fix an optimistic basis.

choices.text: Average the forecast with the sponsor's preferred deadline.
choices.rationale: A desired deadline is not predictive evidence.

choices.text: Exclude past delays before calculating the comparison average.
choices.rationale: Removing real delays can reproduce the planning fallacy.

stem: Two tasks each have a 20% delay probability, and the probability both are delayed is 10%. Which calculation gives the probability of at least one delay?

choices.rationale: This imposes independence contrary to the stated joint probability.
The union rule subtracts the supplied joint probability.
This counts joint delays twice.
This calculates an independent intersection, not the requested union.
This gives the chance of not both being delayed.

stem: An estimate starts near an arbitrary number supplied by an interviewer. Separately, a risk estimate rises because a dramatic example comes easily to mind. Which pair fits, in order?

choices.text: Availability; anchoring
choices.rationale: This reverses the mechanisms.

choices.text: Anchoring; availability
choices.rationale: The first uses a numerical starting point; the second uses ease of recall.

choices.text: Priming; regression to the mean
choices.rationale: The second is not a repeated extreme measurement.

choices.text: Halo; conjunction fallacy
choices.rationale: Neither a global impression nor a probability conjunction is described.

choices.text: Framing; overplacement
choices.rationale: No equivalent descriptions or ranking of personal ability is specified.

stem: A report changes “8% failures” to “92% successes” for the same binary outcome. Another task presents cooking words before an ambiguous word. Which processes are manipulated, respectively?

choices.text: Defaults and anchoring
choices.rationale: No preselected option or initial numerical estimate is manipulated.

choices.text: Semantic priming and framing
choices.rationale: This reverses the described manipulations.

choices.text: Framing and semantic priming
choices.rationale: The first changes equivalent description; the second changes concept accessibility.

choices.text: Loss aversion and overprecision
choices.rationale: Neither outcome demonstrates these particular judgment patterns.

choices.text: Mere exposure and a conjunction error
choices.rationale: Repetition-based liking and intersecting probabilities are not the tasks.

stem: A policy slogan claiming that a reform cuts waiting times is easy to process and repeated often. Its supporters accept it without checking the evidence. Which procedure most directly tests its accuracy?

choices.text: State a falsifiable prediction and examine independent outcome data.
choices.rationale: This replaces fluency and repetition with an evidential test.

choices.text: Compare how much the two sides like their slogans.
choices.rationale: Liking is not a test of the claim.

choices.text: Use a harder font to make the slogan feel less familiar.
choices.rationale: Lower fluency does not itself establish falsity or truth.

choices.text: Ask supporters how natural it sounds.
choices.rationale: Naturalness is another fluency judgment.

choices.text: Repeat it to a larger group and count recognition.
choices.rationale: Recognition measures exposure, not accuracy.

stem: A recruitment panel wants to prevent an engaging interview from dominating unrelated skill judgments. Which scoring procedure best targets this problem?

choices.text: Average repeated overall-impression ratings collected during the same interview.
choices.rationale: Averaging global ratings does not isolate evidence for distinct skills.

choices.text: Give each interviewer an equal vote on the candidate's overall impression.
choices.rationale: Equal voting weights do not address each evaluator's halo effect.

choices.text: Require a longer explanation of the overall impression before scoring dimensions.
choices.rationale: Elaborating the impression may reinforce rather than separate it.

choices.text: Rate job-relevant dimensions separately before recording an overall impression.
choices.rationale: Separate initial ratings constrain spillover from a global evaluation.

choices.text: Record an overall impression first and use it to guide dimension ratings.
choices.rationale: The global judgment may shape each later assessment.

stem: Every application has a final outcome recorded as either success or failure. A report says 3% fail. Which statement gives the complementary frame?

choices.text: 3% of accepted applicants later fail.
choices.rationale: This uses a new conditional denominator and outcome.

choices.text: 97% of those applications succeed.
choices.rationale: Success complements failure within the specified population.

choices.text: 97 applications succeed.
choices.rationale: A count needs the total number of applications to express the same rate.

choices.text: 3% fewer applications fail than last year.
choices.rationale: This introduces a comparison over time absent from the original.

choices.text: 97% of rejected applicants would succeed elsewhere.
choices.rationale: This changes both the population and the outcome.

stem: A trader says a new ritual improves forecasting accuracy. Which test most directly estimates its causal effect on comparable forecasting tasks?

choices.text: Ask successful traders whether they remember using the ritual.
choices.rationale: Selection and retrospective recall bias the comparison.

choices.text: Compare confidence before and after performing the ritual.
choices.rationale: Confidence can change without forecast accuracy changing.

choices.text: Randomly assign ritual and no-ritual trials, then score all forecasts.
choices.rationale: Randomization and complete prospective scoring separate the ritual from selected successes.

choices.text: Compare voluntary ritual users with people who decline it.
choices.rationale: Self-selection may explain performance differences.

choices.text: Compare forecasts before and after the ritual began.
choices.rationale: Changes in task difficulty or experience can confound the comparison.

stem: An applicant resembles a successful engineer. A selection test was validated on experienced engineers, but the current applicant pool consists of novices with a different base rate. What should a probability estimate use?

choices.text: The test's sensitivity as the probability of success after passing.
choices.rationale: This reverses the relevant conditional.

choices.text: Equal prior probabilities because the applicant is unfamiliar.
choices.rationale: Unfamiliarity does not imply a 50–50 base rate.

choices.text: A justified novice reference class and test performance relevant to that class.
choices.rationale: Resemblance alone cannot supply the prior or justify transporting the likelihoods.

choices.text: The number of favorable adjectives in the applicant's description.
choices.rationale: Descriptive detail does not determine diagnostic evidence.

choices.text: The engineer base rate because the applicant matches the prototype.
choices.rationale: Resemblance does not establish membership in the validated population.

stem: The lowest-scoring branches receive coaching and improve next month. Which comparison best tests whether coaching contributed beyond regression to the mean?

choices.text: Attribute every gain after coaching to the intervention.
choices.rationale: Temporal order alone does not isolate the causal contribution.

choices.text: Compare only each coached branch with its own worst month.
choices.rationale: This retains the selection-on-extremes problem.

choices.text: Compare coached low scorers with the highest-scoring branches.
choices.rationale: Different initial selection creates different regression tendencies.

choices.text: Ask coaches to select only branches that later improved.
choices.rationale: Selection on outcomes biases the assessment.

choices.text: Randomly assign similarly low-scoring branches to coaching or control.
choices.rationale: Both groups are selected on low scores, separating treatment from expected regression.

stem: A project succeeds if at least one of two independent components works. Each component works with probability 0.8. Which pair gives equivalent success and failure descriptions for the project?

choices.text: 80% success and 20% failure
choices.rationale: These are individual-component rates.

choices.text: 64% success and 36% failure
choices.rationale: This treats success as requiring both components to work.
